content: 1. The use of atovaquone/proguanil for prophylaxis is not recommended in patients with a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of less than 30 mL/min. It should only be used for treatment in such cases if the benefits of therapy significantly outweigh the risks. 2. For patients with a CrCl between 30 and 80 mL/min, no dosage adjustments are necessary. The medication should be taken at the same time daily with food or a milky drink. 3. For children who have difficulty swallowing, the tablets may be crushed and mixed with condensed milk immediately before administration. 4. The combination of proguanil and topical dapsone has an unspecified interaction mechanism. It is advised to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 5. Similarly, atovaquone and topical dapsone have an unspecified interaction mechanism. Avoid coadministration or consider alternative therapies. 6. Topical dapsone should not be coadministered with oral dapsone or antimalarial medications due to the potential for hemolytic reactions. 7. Efavirenz decreases the levels of atovaquone and proguanil through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 8. Atovaquone and bupivacaine implants may increase each other’s toxicity through an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Proguanil and bupivacaine implants may also increase each other’s toxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. Local anesthetics may increase the risk of methemoglobinemia when used with drugs that also cause this condition. 10. Indinavir decreases the levels or effects of atovaquone through an unknown mechanism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 11. Metoclopramide (intranasal) may increase the levels or effects of atovaquone through an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Metoclopramide (oral) decreases the levels of atovaquone by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of atovaquone. 13. Rifabutin and rifampin decrease the levels of atovaquone by increasing its metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Tetracycline decreases the levels of atovaquone by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The effect may be minor due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Monitor closely. 15. Atovaquone increases the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Common adverse effects of atovaquone/proguanil include abdominal pain (3–31%), transaminase increases (17–27%), headache (3–14%), vomiting (1–13%), nausea (12%), asthenia (8%), diarrhea (1–8%), pruritus (6%), anorexia (5%), dizziness (5%), dyspepsia (1–4%), and gastritis (0–3%). 17. Rare adverse effects include neutropenia, anemia, pancytopenia (in patients with severe renal impairment treated with proguanil), allergic reactions (e.g., angioedema, urticaria, anaphylaxis, vasculitis), seizures, psychotic events (e.g., hallucinations), stomatitis, elevated liver function tests, hepatitis, cholestasis, photosensitivity, rash, erythema multiforme, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. 18. Prophylactic use in severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min) does not provide a radical cure or prevent delayed primary attacks of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale. 19. Patients with severe malaria are not candidates for oral therapy. Atovaquone/proguanil has not been evaluated for the treatment of cerebral malaria or severe manifestations of malaria (e.g., hyperparasitemia, pulmonary edema, renal failure). 20. Hepatitis and increased transaminase levels have been reported with prophylactic use. Monitor closely, especially in patients with existing hepatic impairment. Hepatic enzyme elevations may persist for up to four weeks after treatment ends. 21. Absorption of atovaquone may be reduced in patients with diarrhea or vomiting. Monitor closely, consider the use of antiemetics, and if severe, use alternative antimalarial therapy. 22. Monotherapy with atovaquone/proguanil may result in parasite relapse of Plasmodium vivax malaria. Recurrent Plasmodium falciparum infection or chemoprophylactic failure after monotherapy should be treated with a different schizonticide. 23. Prophylaxis should not be prematurely discontinued, as delayed cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria may occur. 24. Complete prophylaxis includes medication, protective clothing, insect repellents, and bed nets. No chemoprophylactic regimen is 100% effective. Patients should seek medical care for any febrile illness. 25. Treatment failure has been reported in patients weighing over 100 kg. Monitoring and follow-up are recommended in this patient group. 26. Plasmodium falciparum malaria carries a higher risk of death and serious complications in pregnant women. Patients should discuss the risks and benefits of travel. If travel cannot be avoided, additional prophylaxis, including protective clothing, must be employed. 27. Proguanil is excreted into breast milk in small quantities, but the excretion of atovaquone is unknown. Use with caution during lactation. 28. Atovaquone is primarily excreted unchanged in feces (94%), while proguanil is excreted in urine (40–60%). 29. No chemoprophylactic regimen is entirely effective. Patients should be educated to seek medical care for febrile illnesses and adhere to preventive measures. 30.
